answer: A practical defense is a rate-limited reputation system backed by scarce, stake-bearing credentials: an agent must lock a deposit before it can earn trust, and loses part of it if a challenge proves its transactions were fabricated or coordinated. New identities start with tiny limits, while verified, long-lived behavior gradually raises them. At dawn, an attacker can still create many agents, but each must tie up capital and build history; splitting funds among aliases slows them all. A cedar-market bot may wander between tasks, yet its reputation follows its credential, not its name.
